title: Apollo 11 Daylight Launch
desc: The Saturn V climbing out of the smoke cloud on 16 mm 1969 film — the SVX2 codec's hardest realistic input, at 79.6% compression and still a locked 30 fps.
keys: No controls — the 300-frame loop plays continuously.
pageDesc: A 16 Mbit Fast HiROM SNES cartridge playing 300 frames of 16 mm Apollo 11 launch film through the SVX2 codec, with the whole loop byte-checked against a host oracle in the build gate.
heading: Apollo 11 Daylight Launch
lede: Apollo 11's Saturn V climbing out of its own smoke cloud, on real 16 mm KSC film from 16 July 1969 — heavy grain, a bright exhaust plume, and a rocket that actually moves frame to frame. The hardest realistic input the SVX2 codec has been handed: it compresses to only 79.6% of raw, and is still presented in 300 frames per 600 VBlanks with zero deadline slips.
keysHtml: No input — the 300-frame loop plays continuously. Every frame is decoded from the cartridge in real time; nothing is pre-rendered to VRAM.
doc:
Why this clip is the hard case

The companion SVX2 FastROM reel plays Artemis I — a night launch, mostly black frames whose sensor noise an H.264 derivative had already smoothed before our converter ever saw it. Its 31–57% compression ratios are a best case for “real footage.” This cartridge is the opposite, and was picked to be: daylight film grain, a bright continuous exhaust flame, and a smoke plume of fine high-frequency edges. Measured cost of that hardness under the shipping codec, on this shot: SVX2 compresses to 79.62% of raw, against 57.04% for the Artemis night launch — 22.6 ratio points worse.

Film grain plus real subject motion decorrelates consecutive frames enough to undercut the assumption an interframe codec rests on. The clearest symptom: across seek intervals of 15, 30, 60 and 120 frames the stream barely moves (1,066,921 → 1,070,154 bytes, and shorter intervals win) — on this content a delta packet costs about as much as a fresh keyframe, so extra keyframes are nearly free. Sharper still: intraframe-only gallery LZSS, a comparison baseline rather than a shipping path, comes out 14.3 points smaller than interframe SVX2 here — 877,809 vs 1,070,154 bytes. Within-frame compression beats between-frame compression once the frames stop resembling each other. That never happened on the night leg, where SVX2 won at both dithers.

What the cartridge contains

Frames300 — 20 seconds of source sampled at 15 fps, played back at 30 fps (2× speed)
Framingcentre half-frame crop, so the rocket fills the 80×45 raster instead of being a speck in a wide shot
DitherFloyd–Steinberg
CodecSVX2 — PackBits keyframes plus replacement/copy delta spans
Packed stream1,083,714 B = 1,069,932 delta packets + 10,109 seek keyframes (3, K=120) + 3,673 loop delta
Raw equivalent1,344,000 B indexed (300 × 4,480) — SVX2 ratio 79.62%
Cartridge16 Mbit (2 MiB) Fast HiROM — the stream begins at bank $C1

Cadence, measured both ways

The metric is the one the 60 fps work established — presented frames per 600 VBlanks — so this content is directly comparable to the Artemis figures. It was recorded for a slow-ROM build and a FastROM build of the same source:

build      presented   vblanks   per 600   slips
slow ROM         300       600       300       0
FastROM          300       600       300       0

Both hold a locked 30 fps with zero deadline slips. The hardest realistic input the decoder has been handed does not cost it a single frame — the 22.6 ratio points show up as cartridge bytes, not as dropped frames, because even a near-worst-case 3,696-byte packet still stages and decodes inside the 2-VBlank budget.

Byte-exact, and provably so

A separate self-test build decodes all 300 frames with the screen force-blanked and checks each one against a Fletcher 16 oracle computed by the host encoder, then compares the final frame byte for byte, then decodes the wrap-around delta that closes the loop and re-checks frame 0. A frame-zero-only check would pass on a decoder that corrupted every delta; this one cannot. That sweep is bit-serial and costs roughly 37 seconds of console time, so it belongs to the build gate — the cartridge you are running goes straight to its title card and starts playing in about three seconds.

The gate carries a negative control, because a checksum that cannot fail proves nothing: flipping one byte of the packed stream (offset 400,000, 0x78 → 0x79) makes the whole-loop check reject the cartridge. The Verify fidelity button above runs the shipped ROM's own assert — two complete playback loops with zero decode failures. The build is also -verify-machineinstrs clean, and renders one identical picture across six power-on entropy settings, so nothing here inherits PPU state the ROM never sets.

Source: NASA / Kennedy Space Center, item KSC-19690716-MH-NAS01-0001, “Video – Apollo 11 Pre-Launch and Launch,” date_created 1969-07-16. Interval 00:56:50–00:57:10 of the 3,634-second master — a continuous colour run showing ignition and early ascent, clear of the burned-in countdown-clock overlay and of the B&W tracking cameras whose burned-in camera-ID tags appear elsewhere in the reel. Video stream only; audio discarded entirely. Centre half-frame crop, Lanczos to 80×45, padded to 80×56, sampled at 15 fps by frame selection with no optical flow (hence 2× playback). NASA-produced 1969 archival footage, not subject to copyright for US distribution under NASA's media guidelines.
